newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech crown extends rally on Eurobond wave.
newsitem.headline: Czech crown extends rally on Eurobond wave.

text.p: The Czech crown strengthened against its dollar/mark basket on Thursday and was seen moving higher on surging demand caused by a recent wave of crown Eurobond issues, dealers said.

The crown was trading at 27.34 against the dollar and 17.16 against the mark by the middle of the afternoon, putting the Czech currency about 4.4 percent above parity with the Czech National Bank's mark/dollar basket.
Dealers said the rise of the crown was caused, above all, by a wave of new issues of between 15 and 20 billion crowns in eurobonds since the beginning of the year.

"There is definitely a lot of Czech crowns to be bought because this is 20 billion Czech crowns that have been issued and I don't think even half is already executed on the FX side," said Oto Otepka, a bond dealer at ING Barings.
"At least 10 billion must (still) be bought from the FX market."

Otepka added that more upside pressure on the crown was bound to come in the next two to three weeks because the issue dates for the eurobonds were weighted towards the end of Januaray and early February.
"So the major flow of Czech crown buying will come in this period," said Otepka.
Although domestic investors can, in theory, also buy into Eurobonds, they are more interested in the higher yield, despite the higher risk, domestic issues with easier settlement procedures.
This means that almost the entire wave of Eurobonds has been bought up by foreign investors, especially from Germany, Switzerland and Luxembourg, dealers said.
Petr Korous, foreign currency dealer at Ceskoslovenska Obchodni Banka (CSOB) echoed Otepka's opinion that the eurobond issues were the main cause of the crown's appreciation.
However, he also put the crown's gains in the context of a resurgance of interest in emerging markets world wide.
"Globally, all the emerging market currencies are appreciating and all the emerging market stock exchanges' indices are going up...we are just a part of the global picture," he said.

The Czech crown is fixed daily against the mid-point of a basket comprising 35 percent dollars and 65 percent marks. The crown can be fixed by the Czech National Bank (CNB) at up to plus or minus 7.5 percent of the mid-point.
On Thursday, the CNB fixed the crown at 27.354 to the dollar and 17.218 to the mark putting the currency 4.15 percent above the mid-point.
Since the start of 1997 the crown has appreciated by more than two-full percentage points against the basket.
The main underlying reason for foreign ineterest in the Czech crown is the large interest rate differential between the Czech Republic and western countries.
In the middle of 1996 the CNB raised the discount rate to 10.5 percent from 9.5 percent and increased minimum reserve requirements on primary deposits to 11.5 percent from 8.5 percent.
Interbank money market rates up to three months in the Czech Republic hover around 12.5 percent.
